Triggers.value: Talk about people loosing loved ones

Maladaptive Strategies.value: I dwell on how the event could have been prevented
I clean or organise things repeatedly to feel in control
I try to erase the memory of the event

Memory.value: Sometimes I can recall what happened but feel completely numb, as if it happened to a stranger
The memory feels like it is happening right now rather than something that is over
The memory is so extreme it is hard to believe it actually happened to me

Negative Appraisals.value: My beliefs about how the world works have been completely destroyed
The world is a dangerous place
What happened to me was deeply unfair and nothing has been done about it

issues.item: Sexual Objectification: Being looked at sexually
issues.explanation: For a 78-year-old woman whose index trauma is a natural disaster, this trigger is clinically hard to reconcile with the rest of the profile. The other triggers, appraisals, memory items, and strategies all fit disaster-related loss/danger themes, but 'being looked at sexually' implies a sexual-threat/sexual-trauma context that is not represented anywhere else in the formulation or item set. This is more than unusual; it introduces a qualitatively different trauma meaning network without supporting items in Threat, Memory, Appraisals, or Strategies.

vignette: Evelyn, a 78‑year‑old graphic designer who still hovers over a computer screen in the small studio she and her husband share, recalls the night the storm rolled through the coastal town of her youth. The wind howled like a living thing, tearing windows and bending the familiar brick houses into shapes that had never existed before. She was in bed when the first sheets of rain hit the roof, but it was the sudden, deafening roar of the wind that pushed the front door wide open, shattering the fragile calm she had cultivated for years. The memory of that moment is not a single, vivid episode; it is a collage of sensations that feels as if it is happening now, a present‑ticking echo that refuses to leave her mind. She can recall the metallic taste of fear, yet her body feels numb, as though the event had happened to a stranger. The sound of a door slamming, the sight of a broken window, the scent of spilled wine after a neighbor’s party—all have become auditory, visual, and olfactory triggers that yank her back into that night. When she hears a door click in her own home, she feels a rush of dread and immediately begins to think of loss, of loved ones she could have protected. These triggers lead her to shatter her previously stable beliefs about safety and order; she has come to believe the world is a dangerous place where injustice rules. The belief that the storm was utterly unfair, that no one could prevent it, fuels the sense that her life has been violently uprooted. This sense of injustice feeds directly into her negative appraisals, and those appraisals in turn reinforce the triggers that haunt her. Evelyn’s negative appraisal of a dangerous, unfair world pushes her toward maladaptive strategies. She spends hours staring at her desk, counting the lines of a still‑unfinished poster, repeatedly re‑arranging the layout of her tools to feel in control. The compulsive cleaning—she is certain that if she keeps everything perfect, she can ward off another catastrophe—becomes an anchor for her day. She also engages in prevention rumination, constantly replaying how different decisions might have altered the storm’s impact. These rumination sessions deepen her memory of the event, especially the feeling that the story is unreal—she cannot accept that the house, once safe, could have been torn asunder. The more she thinks of the “what ifs,” the more she feels the memory’s emotional numbness intensify, and her body responds by tightening her fingers around the paintbrush. The memory of the night, in turn, fuels her maladaptive strategies. Each time she remembers the door’s sudden opening, she feels compelled to lock every door and window in her home, to check twice, to wash her hands until the water is clear, as if cleaning can erase a trauma. This compulsive cleaning creates a feedback loop: by spending hours in a state of over‑control, she only reinforces the feeling that she is constantly on guard, and her sense of a dangerous world grows more entrenched. The memory’s unreal quality—she cannot believe it happened to her—pushes her to attempt erasing it, to forget it by focusing on bright colors and client briefs, yet the act of memory erasure itself feeds back into the memory, making it more vivid each time she tries to suppress it. The triggers, negative appraisals, maladaptive strategies, and memory weave together into a self‑reinforcing pattern that has dominated her days. She avoids walking down the street at dusk, the last hours of the day when the wind begins to pick up, fearing a sudden gust might crack another window. She even postpones her weekly client calls, telling herself that the thought of a door shutting on her during the conversation would be unbearable. These avoidance behaviors create tangible consequences: her husband has had to take over more responsibilities, and a few of her recent design projects have stalled because she is too anxious to focus. Her sense of shattered beliefs, that the world is an unpredictable and unjust place, now colours every interaction she has, turning even familiar tasks into potential catastrophes. It was the night she finally sat down to finish a brochure for a local charity, when a sudden slam of a door in the hallway made her heart leap so violently she almost lost her composure. She realized that if she could no longer work at her own pace, if her life was controlled by these invisible hands of fear, she needed help. Evelyn’s most pressing fear is that she will never reclaim the sense of control she once had, that her creative mind will remain hostage to the night’s echo. Yet she also holds a fragile hope that with the right support she might learn to separate the storm’s roar from her everyday life, to let the door open without it tearing her world apart.
